title: Judges 10:1–5
context: Two brief reports follow Abimelech’s story. Tola of Issachar rises to save Israel and judges twenty-three years from Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim. Jair the Gileadite judges twenty-two years; his thirty sons ride thirty donkey colts and hold thirty towns in Gilead, known as Havvoth Jair. These short notices contrast with the violent reign before them and come before the longer Ammonite crisis.

verses.text: After Abimelech, Tola the son of Puah, the son of Dodo, a man of Issachar, arose to save Israel. He lived in Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim.
verses.arminianNotes: Tola son of Puah of Issachar arises to save Israel and lives in Shamir. Arminian readers note that the names Tola and Puah also appear as Issachar’s sons in Genesis 46:13, showing family names recurring in the tribe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God raising a deliverer after Abimelech’s chaos, though no enemy is named. Shared ground: the brief report shows God continuing to provide leaders for Israel, in contrast with Abimelech, who seized power for himself.

verses.text: He judged Israel twenty-three years, and died, and was buried in Shamir.
verses.arminianNotes: Tola judges Israel twenty-three years and is buried in Shamir. Arminian readers note that his long tenure suggests a time of stability, recorded without the drama or moral failure seen in many of the longer stories.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in such short notices God’s quiet faithfulness during years the narrator does not describe in detail. Both traditions read Tola’s service as real, even though the book gives few details about his work.

verses.text: After him Jair, the Gileadite, arose. He judged Israel twenty-two years.
verses.arminianNotes: Jair the Gileadite judges Israel twenty-two years. Arminian readers note that leadership now comes from east of the Jordan, anticipating the focus on Gilead in the Ammonite crisis at the end of this chapter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God raising leaders from different tribes and regions across Israel. Shared ground: Jair’s rule is reported briefly, and the text gives no sign of the kind of failure that marked Gideon’s later years or Abimelech’s reign.

verses.text: He had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkey colts. They had thirty cities, which are called Havvoth Jair to this day, which are in the land of Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes: Jair has thirty sons who ride thirty donkey colts and hold thirty cities called Havvoth Jair. Arminian readers note that the text reports this as a mark of status, and many see riding donkeys as a sign of prominence in that period.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the name Havvoth Jair also appears in Numbers 32:41 and Deuteronomy 3:14; how this Jair relates to the earlier one is uncertain. Both traditions read the verse as the text presents it, without speculating further.

verses.text: Jair died, and was buried in Kamon.
verses.arminianNotes: Jair dies and is buried in Kamon. Arminian readers note that Kamon’s location is uncertain, though it is presumably in Gilead, and that the brief burial notice closes his story as simply as Tola’s.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see these short reports as reminders that God’s work continues through leaders whose lives are summarized in a few lines. Shared ground: the notice ends a period of relative calm before Israel falls into idolatry again.
